rss_3_1786818884.title: Einstein the musician, AI prophets and more: Books in brief
rss_3_1786818884.text:
Outsider Animals

Marlene Zuk Princeton Univ. Press (2026)

Evolutionary biologist Marlene Zuk’s charming book begins with a night-time encounter with young raccoons (Procyon lotor) on the deck outside her bedroom in California. They were playing noisily with a hose — and when she tried to shoo them away, one stood up and raised its forelegs, as if inviting her to join in. Zuk calls them outsider animals: “creatures that can intrude upon our lives” but “that don’t need us to survive”. Also included are gulls, cockroaches and coyotes (Canis latrans) — each with its own chapter.

Prophecy

Carissa Véliz Swift (2026)

Prophecy began with divination in ancient Mesopotamia in the third millennium bc. Today, it is integral to predictions made by artificial-intelligence tools, writes philosopher Carissa Véliz in her fascinating, and often worrying, analysis of AI. The close connections between tech bosses and political leaders remind her of the mystic Rasputin’s relationship with Russian tsar Nicholas II. Reliance on AI’s predictions, she argues, takes away our freedom: “Democracy needs uncertainty to thrive.” But philosophy can be an “antidote to prophecy”.

The Powerful Primate

Roland Ennos Scribner (2026)

As an academic, Roland Ennos researched comparative biomechanics: the design and function of animals and plants. Now retired, he has written a formidable history charting how humans learnt to generate increasing power and energy. He argues that industrialization “shaped modern history” by leading to urbanization, transformation of the countryside and globalization. Although Ennos admires this miracle, he accepts it is also devastating, because humans have become “bullies of the natural world”.

Einstein

Brian Foster Oxford Univ. Press (2026)

rss_4_1786818885.title: Undocumented migration does not raise crime rates, huge study finds
rss_4_1786818885.text:
Growing undocumented populations were linked to falling property crime and assaults — but more robberies.Credit: John Moore/Getty

Neighbourhoods across the United States that experienced a growth in their undocumented population also saw property-related and violent crime fall, not rise, according to an analysis of 11,500 neighbourhoods in more than 100 cities.

In a paper published in the Journal of Urban Affairs on 10 August1, researchers combined estimates of numbers of undocumented residents with crime statistics from between 2010 and 2018.

“Our study is the first to analyse these numbers across neighbourhoods and using such a diverse national sample,” says co-author Charis Kubrin, a criminologist at the University of California, Irvine. “That’s important because neighbourhoods are very proximate spaces to people. That’s where perceptions form.”

Earlier studies “have used samples of people or places in a specific jurisdiction”, says Alexis Piquero, a criminologist at the University of Miami in Coral Gables, Florida, but the new work has “a much larger reach”.

The findings support previous research that found no link between immigration and violent crime in the United States and elsewhere. “That very much fits the picture that we’ve seen in UK studies,” says Ben Brindle, a senior researcher with the Migration Observatory project at the University of Oxford, UK.

In the neighbourhood

Undocumented immigrants include people who entered the country illegally or who reside there on an expired visa. The public perception of them is often fuelled by the belief that they are more likely to commit crimes than are documented immigrants or citizens.

But, Piquero notes, “it’s very hard to measure the number of undocumented immigrants in any country because they’re undocumented. So, researchers have come up with estimates.”

In the current study, Kubrin and her colleagues were granted access to non-public demographic data for 46 million people through a US federal statistical research data center.

To estimate the number of undocumented immigrants, the researchers excluded people who were recorded to be US citizens or born in the country, as well as those who were recorded as receiving public health insurance, enrolled in higher education or married to a US citizen — because these individuals are likely to be authorized visa holders or permanent residents.

The analysis found that, on average, 5.6% of residents in a neighbourhood were undocumented in 2010, and that this dropped to 4.8% in 2018. “Our estimates are quite similar to [those of] the Department of Homeland Security,” says Kubrin.

Human migration has surged since 2000 — these maps reveal where people are going

The researchers then mapped the proportion of undocumented immigrants across neighbourhoods, using crime data from the National Incident Crime Study. Kubrin and her colleagues focused on violent crimes — which included homicides, robberies and aggravated assaults — as well as the property crimes such as burglaries and motor-vehicle thefts.

Their analysis revealed that increases in undocumented immigrant populations were associated with lower levels of property crimes and aggravated assaults.

Robberies, however, tended to rise in neighbourhoods with increased undocumented populations. “It could be that crime rates are higher in some neighbourhoods because immigrants are victims rather than offenders,” says Kubrin. Undocumented immigrants are more likely to get paid in cash and less likely to have bank accounts than are other residents, which could put them at a greater risk of being robbed, for instance.

rss_6_1786818888.title: Author Correction: Cretaceous bird from Brazil informs the evolution of the avian skull and brain
rss_6_1786818888.text:
In the originally published version of our article, the endocranial landmark configuration from the enantiornithine bird Navaornis hestiae included nine misplaced patch semilandmarks resulting from a sharp corner in the three-dimensional model, which inadvertently shifted those semilandmarks to the next solid surface along the landmark’s normal trajectory. Here, we amend this problem by repositioning these misplaced coordinates using the software Stratovan Checkpoint (the state-of-the-art licensed and maintained version of the software used in our original manuscript: IDAV Landmark Editor) and upload the corrected dataset to the link provided in the Data availability section in the original article. We produced an updated principal components plot summarizing patterns of endocranial shape with the corrected dataset (Fig. 1). Patterns are unchanged regarding the ‘intermediate’ morphology of N. hestiae along PC1, the main axis of endocranial shape variation. However, with the corrected dataset, N. hestiae falls within the crown bird dispersion along PC2, whereas in the initially published article, N. hestiae fell just outside crown bird variation along the same axis. The amount of shape variation explained by each principal component in the corrected dataset varies slightly from the values in the original article; however, our interpretations of avian endocranial evolution are unaltered by this relatively minor change. To further reassess our initial interpretations, we calculated total shape distances (Procrustes distances) from Navaornis hestiae to all the taxa included in our sample (Fig. 2). The six closest species in endocranial shape include the stem bird Archaeopteryx, the unnamed troodontid IGM 100/1126, and crown birds such as Ptilinopus (Columbiformes), Cariama (Cariamiformes), Crypturellus (Palaeognathae, Tinamiformes) and Caloenas (Columbiformes). This assortment of taxa highlights the combination of plesiomorphic and crown bird-like traits in the endocranial morphology of N. hestiae, as originally interpreted. We thank Jesús Marugán-Lobón and Jingmai O’Connor, whose queries helped us identify issues with the original dataset. We also thank Patrick O’Connor and three anonymous reviewers who helped us improve the text of this correction notice.

Fig. 1: Navaornis and endocranial evolution in birds and non-avian dinosaurs. Full size image (a) Three-dimensional principal component (PC) morphospace (PC1 versus PC2, and PC1 versus PC3) of cranial endocasts from crown birds, Archaeopteryx, Navaornis and relevant non-avian taxa. Principal component plots are scaled to the same ratio, so distances are the same on the x axis and y axis. Along PC1, Navaornis falls in an intermediate position between stemward taxa such as Archaeopteryx and crown birds, whereas it falls within the range of crown bird variation along PC2 and PC3. (b) Shape changes associated with scores representing the 5th and 95th quantiles from each of the three main PCs of endocranial shape. Plus (+) and minus (−) symbols indicate whether shape warps are associated with positive or negative scores along each axis. Landmarks are colour-coded for the main brain regions. Brown arrows in b depict the foramen magnum orientation. Percentages in parentheses in a and b indicate the proportion of total shape variance explained by each of the principal components. This figure represents a correction of the PCA plots in Fig. 4b and Extended Data Fig. 10d from the original article.

rss_7_1786818889.title: How to make your science business succeed when you’re a female founder
rss_7_1786818889.text:
Emma Yates, chief scientific officer at Proteotype Diagnostics, would like to see more funding and support for founders during parental leave. Credit: Wesley Sukdao, Proteotype CEO

An estimated 25 million women across the world’s most advanced economies are being denied the opportunity to launch and develop their own businesses, and those who do typically have more-modest growth ambitions than male founders, finds a report by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD)1.

According to the Bridging the Finance Gap for Women Entrepreneurs report, published at the end of last year, the gender gap in start-up financing is particularly stark in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) sectors. The OECD trawled studies from 2013 onwards, with a focus on ones from the past few years, finding that, globally, companies founded by women receive only about 2% of total venture-capital investments.

Female entrepreneurs are about 63% less likely to secure venture-capital funding than are men, and on average get only 70% of the amount that male entrepreneurs receive. This means that they are less likely to seek loans or investment in the first place, the report warns. One estimate in the report speculates that UK gross domestic product could have been 12% larger than it was in 2017 if women had started and scaled up businesses at the same rate as men did.

How I honed my biopharma dealmaking and business-development skills after my PhD

A second report on venture-capital allocation published last year paints a similar picture. It found that of the US$289 billion invested globally in 2024, 2.3% went to female-only founding teams, compared with 83.6% to all-male teams. Mixed-gender teams landed a 14.1% share of the funding pot.

The report, which was published by the London-based entrepreneur-support community the Founders Forum Group, also revealed that during fundraising women are more than twice as likely as male founders to be asked questions focused on risks. They are also interrupted almost five times more frequently than men are during pitch presentations and spend an average of 7.4 months fundraising compared with 5.2 months for their male counterparts.

The findings from these two reports will resonate with many female science entrepreneurs and those who support them. Four women tell Nature about their experiences learning to navigate a funding landscape in an ecosystem that can often seem hostile.

Worst critics

“Most of my investor conversations have been constructive and professional,” says Emma Yates, chief scientific officer at Proteotype Diagnostics in Cambridge, UK. She co-founded the company with her husband, its chief executive and chairperson, in 2019. “There have been isolated moments where I felt assumptions were being made that a male founder might not have faced, and a few investors were also uncomfortable with a husband-and-wife founding team,” Yates adds.

The company’s mission is to create an affordable early-cancer detection method based on the body’s immune response. So far, the firm has raised around $6.89 million in private and grant funding and the test is currently in a clinical trial, the final results of which are due at the end of the year. After that, Yates expects that they will start to seek series A funding — the first substantial round of start-up venture-capital financing — to take the company forwards.

In Yates’s view, female founders are often their own worst critics, which can make them less likely to seek funding for a good idea before they have a huge amount of evidence to back it up. “In science, you are trained to be cautious and to let the evidence speak,” she says. “Fundraising also requires you to communicate the scale of the opportunity before every uncertainty is removed. That was a learning curve for me.”

Ultimately, Yates thinks that “the bigger question now is whether women founders receive the same benefit of the doubt and access to growth capital”.

Careers advice from scientists in industry

Last year she received a £75,000 ( US$101,000) Women and Innovation Award from Innovate UK, the country’s national innovation agency, which Yates used to complete manufacturing validation of Proteotype’s diagnostic kit.

Business-development help came from other programmes. “The most useful support was very specific,” says Yates. It was crucial for “helping us think through clinical-study design, the technical evidence base, investor communication, commercial development and how to build the right plan around the science”.

In 2022, Yates had her first child. “Typically at that point in time, you’re wanting something with lots of job security so you can take a nice one-year maternity leave,” she says of the standard parental-leave practice in the United Kingdom. At the time, Proteotype still depended heavily on the founding team. “I was back on video calls within five weeks,” she says. “For founders, especially in science-based companies, the choice is often not a clean binary between being fully off or fully back at work.”

Yates would like to see innovation grants and founder-support programmes that provide temporary operational cover and childcare during parental leave. “For an early-stage science company, that kind of support could be the difference between maintaining momentum and a founder feeling they have to come back before they are ready,” she says.

Making the jump from a research career to founding her own company has been life changing for Yates. “I’m a different person than I was when I started,” she says. “I know how to lead a team, work with investors and clinical stakeholders, and make decisions under uncertainty. That is what science-based entrepreneurship requires.”

Perfectionism

Henriette Maaß, co-founder and chief executive of NanoStruct in Würzburg, Germany, credits the company’s foundation to a transfer grant from Germany’s Federal Ministry for Economic Affairs and Energy. The company uses gold nanostructures to detect small quantities of contaminants, such as bacteria in the food industry. The grant enabled her to leave a project-management role at a semiconductor firm in 2021 and return to The Julius Maximilians University of Würzburg (where she completed her physics PhD two years earlier). There, she worked with Enno Schatz, a former colleague who would become chief technology officer at NanoStruct, to develop the idea that led to her co-founding the company.

More grants, including a €75,000 ($86,000) award from the European Union’s Women TechEU programme — which supports start-ups founded or co-founded by women who hold a top management position and own at least 25% of company shares — enabled the company to keep going. It now has ten employees and is looking for funding to take its product to market.

Henriette Maaß, co-founder and chief executive of NanoStruct, used government and European Union funding to launch and sustain her company.Credit: Enno Schatz

Maaß was pregnant when she started seeking early ‘seed’ funding for NanoStruct in 2025, and worried about how both potential funders and colleagues would react. “This was actually something I felt a bit insecure about but I knew I wanted to stay as chief executive of my company,” she says. She began to see the positive side of at least knowing they would attract investors who would be comfortable with a chief executive who is also a new mother.

Now, Maaß often takes her baby to meetings. “There is no one-fits-all advice,” she says. “Find your own way to manage both roles and don’t expect yourself to be perfect.”

Transitions

A key challenge faced by Kitiya Vongkamjan, chief executive at Unique Phage-Based Solutions (UniFAHS), was how to quickly turn herself from an academic into a businesswoman. She co-founded the Bangkok-based biotechnology company — which uses phage technology to target major food-borne pathogens — in 2020 with Chalita Wongpukdee, who is now the company’s chief marketing officer.

“We need to go from researchers to founders, and the ecosystem is so different” between the two sectors, says Vongkamjan. She thinks it takes courage for researchers to make that switch.

Vongkamjan received a Leaders in Innovation Fellowship from the UK Royal Academy of Engineering, which included a two-week entrepreneurship training course. At the end of the course, participants showcased their innovations in front of a panel of judges. Vongkamjan says that this taught her “all the skills for research to commercialization” and provided her with a mentor for the first two years of developing her spin-off. Financial help also came from the “three Fs”, Vongkamjan jokes — friends, family and fools — alongside commercialization support from start-up incubators at the Southern Regional Science Park at the Prince of Songkla University in Hay Yai, Thailand. Vongkamjan held an academic position there from 2012 to 2020. Her current institution, Kasetsart University in Bangkok, has also been supportive.

Meet the biotech-company founders driven by their child’s rare disease

In Asia, venture-capital funding often seems “out of reach” for women, says Vongkamjan, which might explain why her company didn’t progress as quickly as some of the companies that have a male founder, she adds. “People want to know, are you really a business person, or are you really just a research-focused person?”

Vongkamjan says that she has noticed women are also less likely to talk-up their successes. For example, she has been reticent to post about milestones reached by her business but says, “if you go on LinkedIn and you compare female and male founders, you see more posts” from the men. In 2025, a group of women even showed anecdotally, by posting with male aliases, that women’s LinkedIn posts tend to get less traffic than men’s do.

In 2024, UniFAHS completed a funding round of $1.4 million to move into other markets across southeast and South Asia. Funding came partly from ADB Ventures, an investment fund that Vongkamjan says has a reputation for supporting women. The company now employs 20 people but Vongkamjan has chosen to keep her food-microbiology laboratory at Kasetsart University, where she continues research that feeds into the company. She anticipates that will change as the company grows and everything will eventually be conducted in the company’s lab.

rss_8_1786818890.title: Can Anthropic’s invisible watermarks curb ‘AI slop’? Researchers remain sceptical
rss_8_1786818890.text:
The AI company Anthropic says that its Claude models will label AI-generated content with a watermark.Credit: Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty

Anthropic, the firm behind the artificial-intelligence model Claude, has announced that text generated by any models launched on or after 2 August will be invisibly embedded with a watermark that indicates the output was written by AI. Meanwhile, images generated by Claude will in most cases come with metadata that contains a digital signature to show that the model processed the file.

Text-based watermarks use an algorithm to tweak how an AI model selects its wording. When applied to a stretch of text, this process leaves a statistically observable trace in the output. Anthropic, based in San Francisco, California, says that its watermark won’t change the “meaning, quality, or readability of Claude’s response” and that the mark “may persist through some editing”.

The move comes in response to the EU AI Act, which was formally adopted in 2024. As of 2 August this year, providers of frontier AI models must ensure that AI-generated outputs are detectable, or be hit with fines of up to €15 million (about US$17 million) or 3% of their global annual turnover. Models released after 2 August will have to meet the requirements immediately, whereas versions already on the market have until 2 December to do so. Anthropic says that watermarks will be applied on Claude’s outputs worldwide.

The presence of the watermark reveals little about how the model was used. Detecting one “provides a signal” that content was made with Claude, says Anthropic, but is not conclusive: the model might have been used just to summarize or translate an original human idea, for example. Equally, a lack of a watermark doesn’t mean that the text was not generated by AI. Because the watermarks are based on patterns of subtle changes in a model’s word choice, passages that are very short, or that have been paraphrased or rewritten, might no longer carry a signal.

‘Humanizer’ tool can erase signs of AI-written text — alarming scientists

The impact that such watermarks will have on academic integrity remains unclear. Given that watermarks can be stripped from text easily — for example, by using another model — they are unlikely to stop motivated people from using AI to produce fake or low-quality papers, known as AI slop, says Reese Richardson, a metascientist at Northwestern University in Evanston, Illinois.

But if AI firms create tools that allow others to check for the watermark — as Anthropic has said it will do — and if these tools have an acceptably low rate of false positives, some illegitimate uses of AI could be detected, says computer scientist Nihar Shah, who studies the evaluation of science at Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania.

Watermarks could, for example, help journal editors or conference organizers to enforce strict ‘no AI’ policies in peer reviews, as the International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML) 2026 did in one of its two possible review streams. Organizers of the July event added a watermark to papers distributed for peer review that generated telltale text when AI was used in review reports. They caught 506 reviewers who violated the no-AI policy. “This experience suggests that while some illegitimate AI uses may be done carefully to evade detection, many others may simply copy-paste AI outputs,” says Shah, who was behind the ICML’s watermarking process.

Invisible ink

rss_9_1786818891.title: AI isn’t ready to research itself
rss_9_1786818891.text:
One of the earliest applications of ‘AI scientists’ was to research AI itself.Credit: La Pico de Gallo/Getty

Artificial intelligence has made leaps in AI research itself, finding ways to make existing algorithms smarter — or writing new ones. But computers are not yet ready to replace their makers, according to a study posted on the preprint server arXiv1 in late July.

“I don’t think full automation of open-ended research is on the horizon right now,” says Sayash Kapoor, a computer scientist at Princeton University in New Jersey and a co-author of the preprint.

The effort to fully automate the scientific process, from idea generation to the writing and self-evaluation of a paper, was pioneered by a team mostly from the firm Sakana AI in Tokyo. The team unveiled their system, called The AI Scientist, in 2024, and later published results from an improved version in March in Nature2.

The AI Scientist was tasked with studying pitfalls in machine learning. Three of the papers it produced were submitted for peer review at a conference workshop, and one achieved a score high enough for acceptance. But, according to Kapoor, peer review is an unreliable way of assessing the quality of a paper, especially in AI research.

More generally, some researchers have questioned whether automating AI research from idea creation to publication can produce true breakthroughs yet, suggesting it is better at optimizing existing techniques.

To hold AI to a higher standard than peer review, Kapoor and his colleagues created a new challenge, called shadow evaluation. First, they picked two papers that had been submitted to this year’s Neural Information Processing Systems conference. Then they asked an AI tool to do research and write papers based on a research question from each paper, and asked the original authors to scrutinize its output. The idea was that these authors would have more of the expertise and dedication to dig into the output than a harried peer reviewer would.

The team built its AI system by ‘harnessing’ the large language model Claude Opus 4.8 in a modified version of the agentic system OpenClaw, and then wrapped that in a broader ‘scaffold’ that contained general instructions and ways to check progress. The harness gave the model an array of tools, including the ability to create sub-agents and to access the Internet, software libraries, computer processors for running experiments and software that simulates peer review. For each paper, the AI system had six days and US$3,000 in computing credits. Following the general research direction of the first paper, Kapoor’s team asked the system to design a method for the precise control of chatbot personality. Mirroring the second paper, it had to design a failure detector for a certain kind of neural network.

The authors were surprised by the system’s success at the engineering work of its research. It could run hundreds of experiments over several days, without getting stuck in a loop of unresolvable errors. And it performed solid literature reviews and made some minor findings. It also caught its own false claims (sometimes called hallucinations) and did not try to cut corners (or ‘reward hack’), despite the authors’ predictions.

Poor marks

But the AI system mostly failed at its two assigned tasks, earning overall scores of 2/6 and 1/6 from the original papers’ authors. A typical way in which it would fail was to select a few hypotheses to explore, but settle too early on one and not backtrack sufficiently when its approach wasn’t working. Subsequent self-review wasn’t sufficiently negative, so the system persisted on its initial choices, whittling down its claims until it said little of interest.

rss_10_1786818892.title: Why China should reassess how it rewards young scientists
rss_10_1786818892.text:
China’s research sector has experienced spectacular growth over the past two decades. The increase in scientific output is due, in part, to a system that funnelled resources to researchers selected by prestigious talent-acquisition schemes. This approach has helped the nation’s scientists to publish in leading journals. Yet, a rapid expansion in the scientific workforce has also created a widening divide between a small group of leading academics and the rest of the nation’s research community, including growing numbers of young scientists who are competing for limited resources.

The prestigious titles available to leading Chinese researchers are commonly known as academic ‘hats’, and are earned through participation in national talent programmes, elite early-career scientist schemes and provincial and municipal initiatives. Having the correct hat can influence everything from salary and access to laboratory space to promotion prospects. Thus, for many early-career researchers, success tends to depend not only on scientific ability but also on securing one of these coveted designations.

Why China needs to review its approach to research evaluation

The Chinese government increasingly acknowledges the unintended consequences of this system. In June, Qiushi, the official journal of the Chinese Communist Party, published an influential article calling for the nation’s talent-development strategy to be reformed (see go.nature.com/45nd8hh). One sentence stood out to early-career researchers like myself: academic titles and talent labels should return to their “academic and honorary nature”, rather than being used mechanically to decide salaries and allocate resources. The statement reflects growing concern that a system that was originally designed to identify and reward excellence has evolved into one that distorts incentives and concentrates opportunities among a select few.

The scramble for funding and the intense pressures facing early-career academics are hardly unique to China. But the competition is amplified by the sheer scale of the nation’s talent pipeline. Chinese universities and research institutions admitted roughly 171,000 doctoral students in 2024, compared with around 54,000 in 2005 — an increase of more than 200%. Owing to intense competition, academic hats have become a convenient administrative shortcut for deciding who receives support.

Move beyond ‘publish or perish’ by measuring behaviours that benefit academia

China’s tenure-track system is often presented as an adaptation of US and European models. In practice, it functions differently. Hired faculty members are typically evaluated for three to six years against an array of demanding targets — including numbers of publications in specific journals and successful grant applications, teaching performance and which talent titles they have obtained.

rss_11_1786818893.title: Daily briefing: New evidence of the mysterious ‘glueballs’
rss_11_1786818893.text:
Physicists have found evidence of a particle made entirely of force-carrying gluons. Plus, what changes to US vaccine recommendations mean for children and the ways food scientists are improving chocolate.

Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.

Glueballs are made of gluons, which bind quarks to form protons and neutrons.Credit: Sefa kart/Getty

A team of physicists says it has observed strong evidence of a mysterious ‘glueball’, a particle made up of force-carrying gluons. The team says that a particle known as X(2370) is mostly made up of these glueballs — clusters of the gluons that bind quarks to form protons and neutrons and hold them inside the nucleus of an atom. There is no single smoking gun that proves that this particle is made of glueballs, says particle physicist Bruce Yabsley. But the findings are “quite persuasive”, he says. The group presented their results at the International Conference on High Energy Physics in Natal, Brazil, last week.

Nature | 5 min read

An executive order signed by US President Donald Trump this week calls for children in the United States to be vaccinated against fewer diseases, and recommends that combination shots be split into individual jabs that are spread out over time — starting with the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine. The order is “not in any sense grounded in science”, says viral immunologist Paul Offit. The order instructs the country’s top health officials to adopt its recommendations, but it does not have any inherent legal power. Implementing the recommendations would require vaccine companies to manufacture jabs that target each illness individually, which could take years and cost hundreds of millions of dollars.

Nature | 6 min read

The world’s oceans are on the brink of setting an all-time heat record, reaching temperatures that could roil marine ecosystems and sap the ocean’s ability to take up carbon dioxide from the air. Sea surface temperatures have already broken records for the past two months — boosted by human-induced climate change and a powerful El Niño event growing in the Pacific Ocean. The average surface temperature is now hovering just a few hundredths of a degree below the current record from March 2024. “It just spells trouble for the planet,” says climate scientist Kristina Dahl.

Nature | 5 min read

Source: Copernicus Climate Change Service/European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts

Features & opinion

In Rwampara, Democratic Republic of the Congo, the medical charity Alima runs a temporary hospital ward to treat people with Ebola, amid the outbreak rapidly spreading in the country. The centre has treated more than 700 people so far, 291 have died from their illness. Only infected people and health workers are allowed to step onto the ward, but the protective clothing that medical staff wear isn’t always enough to protect them from the virus. In July, there was a strike in Rwampara over unpaid wages that included health workers and support staff, leaving many patients without care for several days.

The New York Times | 5 min read

How do you select a final grant proposal when the options all have pretty much the same score? You do what the ancient Greeks did when they couldn’t make a decision — trust in chance. This lottery system can help attract a more diverse pool of proposals and take the pressure off funders flooded with applications, proponents argue. But some critics think that using a lottery to select grants overlooks important context, such as how a proposal fits into the wider literature. Still, the idea isn’t as radical as it might seem. “It’s something that multiple cultures have used and that most people understand as intrinsically fair,” says statistician Adrian Barnett.

Nature | 13 min read

More than 175 years after it was first unveiled, there are still ways in which chocolate can be improved, say food scientists. Some are analysing the microbes involved in the fermentation of cocoa beans to determine which combinations might be responsible for flavour notes in the final product. Others are experimenting with ultrasound waves that alter the treat’s texture, or digging into the crystal structure of fat blooms — the white splotches that can appear on chocolate — to determine what causes them to form.

Knowable | 8 min read

rss_12_1786818895.title: Ancient rise in CO<sub>2</sub> was catastrophic for forests: what that means for today’s plants
rss_12_1786818895.text:
Satellite data shows a browning trend across the planet since around the turn of the century. Credit: ezypix/Getty

Around 56 million years ago, a sharp rise in carbon dioxide in the atmosphere led to severe global warming that transformed the planet’s surface. A detailed reconstruction of an ancient ecosystem suggests that this transformation included a widespread decline in forest cover. The study1, published in Science on 13 August, has parallels for what could happen as a result of human-driven climate change, say the authors.

“We’re seeing that now all over the world. Many forests are in states of decline,” says co-author Regan Dunn, a palaeoclimatogist at the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County in California.

This sudden warming event, called the Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum (PETM), was one of the most notable climatic upheavals in Earth’s history. The volume of CO 2 released during that period is thought to be roughly equivalent to the total human emissions that would be released by the end of the twenty-first century under a pessimistic scenario. The ancient surge of CO 2 raised global average temperatures by between 5 and 9 °C, changing the climate for more than 150,000 years.

Using fossils, sediments and other geochemical evidence preserved from this time, researchers have begun to piece together a picture of abrupt changes to Earth’s ecosystems that took place in response to this warming. The make-up of forests changed, with broad-leafed trees in the mid-latitudes giving way to landscapes dominated by ferns. Rivers supercharged by a water-logged atmosphere carried away more sediment. Soils stored less carbon.

Dunn and her colleagues sought to get a clearer view of how these shifts changed the structure of forest canopies. This can reveal information about changes in carbon storage in ecosystems, says Dunn. “It’s really telling you something about how the forest is functioning.”

The ancient analysis was aimed at shedding light on a question ecologists have today: how will Earth’s ecosystems respond to rising levels of CO 2 ? Higher concentrations of the greenhouse gas trap more heat, boosting temperatures and shifting patterns of precipitation in ways that can stress plants. However, more CO 2 also acts to fertilize plants, and there’s wide uncertainty about how these opposing forces will affect forests of the future.

Reading the leaves

To work out the structure of ancient forests, the team analysed the shape of fossilized leaf cells in sediment cores from the Hanna Basin in Wyoming. Because of the way plants grow and stretch towards light, the shape of these cells offers a measure of how much of the canopy was shaded versus how much was exposed to sunlight. “There’s this difference between sun leaves and shade leaves, even on the same plant,” says Dunn.

The researchers used the fossil leaves to estimate how canopies changed at the Wyoming site across the PETM, as CO 2 rose and temperature changed. The ‘greenness’ of the forest was described by a metric called the leaf area index.

The forest didn’t fare well, they found. After an initial rise in canopy coverage at the start of the PETM, the leaf area saw a steep drop of 61% over the next few thousand years. Then, canopy cover remained 35% lower for tens of thousands of years, until the end of the PETM.

rss_13_1786818896.title: Will the mRNA flu shot work better than a regular seasonal one? What the science says
rss_13_1786818896.text:
The number of influenza infections could be reduced by an mRNA vaccine.Credit: Science Photo Library

On 5 August, the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) granted approval to Moderna’s mRNA-based flu vaccine, mFLUSIVA, for adults aged 50–64, and accelerated approval for adults aged 65 and older. Moderna say it will be available “in a few weeks” to be rolled out for the 2026–27 flu season in the United States.

Researchers welcomed the decision, noting that the vaccine’s mRNA platform allows it to be rapidly reformulated to match circulating influenza strains. “This approval is very important and can be a great game changer” because the platform could help solve the problem of slow manufacturing, says Emanuele Montomoli, a researcher in hygiene and public health at the University of Siena, Italy.

The vaccine is also being reviewed by regulatory agencies in the European Union, Canada and Australia. A related product has already been permitted for use in Europe: in April, the European Commission approved Moderna’s combined seasonal influenza and COVID-19 mRNA vaccine mCombriax.

Tests on more than 20,000 adults showed that 2% of people who received the mFLUSIVA vaccine (called mRNA-1010 before FDA approval) developed a laboratory-confirmed case of flu, verified through testing and symptoms reports1. By comparison, 2.8% of those who received a standard dose of a comparator non-mRNA vaccine developed symptoms.

The tangled history of mRNA vaccines

“The key questions regarding immunogenicity, efficacy and safety have been addressed, which enabled the licensure of mFLUSIVA,” said Raffael Nachbagauer, vice-president of infectious-disease research at Moderna in Cambridge, Massachusetts, who is involved in mFLUSIVA trials.

But scientists still have questions about how this vaccine will perform when it’s rolled out to millions of people. Moderna has agreed with the FDA to conduct a confirmatory phase IV trial to research the efficacy relative to an enhanced vaccine in people aged 65 and older, says Nachbagauer.

Better flu immunity?

The mFLUSIVA vaccine works by delivering mRNA molecules encoding the flu virus’s hemagglutinin surface protein, packaged in a lipid nanoparticle that carries it into cells. Cells then translate the mRNA into hemagglutinin protein, which the immune system recognizes and subsequently builds antibodies against.

Clinical studies evaluating the efficacy of mFLUSIVA found that it had a 26.6% relative reduction in confirmed flu cases compared with a standard influenza vaccine. The investigation tested antigens from the three 2024–25 strains that were recommended by the World Health Organization in time for the corresponding Northern Hemisphere influenza season.

The study also found that mFLUSIVA was well tolerated by most participants. Adverse side effects were predominantly mild to moderate, with injection-site pain, fatigue and headache the most frequently reported. Side effects were more common in people who received the mRNA vaccine versus a standard dose vaccine — for example, injection-site pain was reported more than twice as often with mFLUSIVA as with the standard-dose comparator.

The ghost of influenza past and the hunt for a universal vaccine

A separate study2 in people over the age of 65 comparing mFLUSIVA with licensed comparators contributed to mFLUSIVA’s accelerated approval in the 65-and-older age group. It measured participants’ antibody responses to flu rather than flu-like symptoms, and found that a single dose of the mRNA flu vaccine produced a stronger antibody response than did existing standard-dose and high-dose flu shots.

“A relative improvement over a standard-dose influenza vaccine is already clinically meaningful,” says Federico Martinón-Torres, head of paediatrics at the University Clinical Hospital of Santiago de Compostela, Spain.
